hints: Focus on what the ammonium ion needs to turn into ammonia gas, think acid or base?
Remember that $\text{NH}_4^+$ releases $\text{NH}_3$ only when it reacts with $\text{OH}^-$ ions on warming.
Check the list again and pick out the only reagent that is strongly alkaline and provides hydroxide ions.
walkthrough:
**Recall the test for ammonium ions**

Think of $\text{NH}_4^+$ as a hidden store of ammonia. To free the ammonia, you need a base to remove $\text{H}^+$ from it.

General rule:
$$\text{NH}_4^+ + \text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{NH}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$

**Identify which reagent is a base**

Limewater is aqueous calcium hydroxide, $\text{Ca}(\text{OH})_2$. It is alkaline and supplies lots of $\text{OH}^-$ ions.

Reaction with heating:
$$2\text{NH}_4^+ + \text{Ca}(\text{OH})_2 \rightarrow \text{Ca}^{2+} + 2\text{NH}_3 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$$

**Conclude the answer**

Warming ammonium sulfate with limewater liberates ammonia gas, which turns damp red litmus blue. None of the other reagents can do this.

options.A: Aqueous bromine is an oxidising agent used to test for alkenes, not a base. It provides no $\text{OH}^-$ ions, so it cannot deprotonate $\text{NH}_4^+$ to form $\text{NH}_3$.
options.B: Dilute hydrochloric acid provides $\text{H}^+$ ions, which is the opposite of what is needed. Adding acid to an ammonium salt keeps it as $\text{NH}_4^+$ and no ammonia is liberated.
options.C: Limewater is $\text{Ca}(\text{OH})_2(aq)$, a base. On heating with $(\text{NH}_4)_2\text{SO}_4$ it reacts: $(\text{NH}_4)_2\text{SO}_4 + \text{Ca}(\text{OH})_2 \rightarrow \text{CaSO}_4 + 2\text{NH}_3 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$. This is the classic test for ammonium ions.
options.D: Acidified potassium dichromate(VI) is a strong oxidising agent used to test for reducing agents. It is acidic, not alkaline, so it will not convert $\text{NH}_4^+$ into $\text{NH}_3$.
